Welcome to the Millbrook woodcarving weekend! We're so glad you've come to try something with your hands. No experience is needed here — just curiosity and a willingness to make a few friendly mistakes along the way. Everything you need will be provided, so settle in, ask lots of questions, and don't worry about getting it perfect; wood is forgiving, and so are we. See you at the workbench!

1. Gamify it: race the clock with a timer and try to beat your record, or turn it into a game show where wrong answers cost points and streaks earn double.
2. Shuffle and remix: sort the deck by how well you know each card (three piles: easy,.medium, hard), then only drill the hard pile until cards migrate up. Watching a card climb piles is weirdly satisfying.
3. Say it out loud, theatrically: answer in a dramatic movie-trailer voice, sing tough ones, or explain the concept to an imaginary class without peeking. Silly voices lock facts into memory better than silent reading — and make the grind feel like a performance!

1. Speed round: rapid-fire questions, 15 seconds each, anyone can steal the answer if the first person stalls.

4. Pop quiz bingo: everyone predicts what the teacher will test, and correct predictions earn points toward snack-buying privileges.

Rotate who runs each round so nobody zones out, and add a timer for urgency!

Start with "pass the applause": everyone stands in a circle and claps toward the next person, so the clap races around the room — instant laughter, zero pressure. Then try "hum the chorus": play a well-known song and have everyone hum along together, so their voices fill the space before anyone solos. A quick "two truths and a talent" round works well too — kids share two facts and one hidden ability, which sneaks in a mini-announcement of their act. Finish with a group countdown chant where the whole room cheers one volunteer on stage for ten seconds; the audience learns to be loud and supportive, and the first performer discovers the crowd is on their side!
